summary: A brick tower on an islet in the Savannah River, lit from 1849 to 1909 to mark the South Channel below Fort Pulaski. Closed to the public today.

structures.note: First brick daymark tower, built 1837 to 1839 (NPS); destroyed by the 1854 hurricane.
Rebuilt on the same foundation. The USLHS gives 1857 and LighthouseFriends 1856 for the tower.

access.note: The National Park Service says the lighthouse and its island are closed to the public. An overlook trail is on land; a boat or kayak is needed to get close.

facts.agency: National Park Service (Fort Pulaski National Monument)

events.note: First congressional appropriation for a light here, per the 1934 Bulletin. LighthouseFriends gives 1832.
First brick daymark tower, built March 1837 to November 1839.
Oyster Beds and Cockspur beacons established (LighthouseFriends). NPS dates the contract for an illuminated station to 1848.
Tower rebuilt on the same foundation (NPS; Bulletin 1934 gives restorations in 1855). LighthouseFriends gives 1856; USLHS gives 1857.
Original optic: sixth-order Fresnel (USLHS). LighthouseFriends gives a fifth-order lens in 1856.
Light temporarily extinguished at the start of the Civil War.
Union bombardment of Fort Pulaski with the tower in the line of fire; minor damage to the tower.
Relit and painted white as a daymark, 25 April 1866.
Keepers' dwelling struck by lightning in April 1880 (LighthouseFriends); the Bulletin says the dwelling was again out of repair.
The August 1881 storm surge destroyed the keeper's residence.
Great hurricane of 1893; the keepers sheltered in the northwest stair tower of Fort Pulaski.
Keepers' quarters moved into a converted dwelling atop Fort Pulaski.
Transferred from the Coast Guard to the National Park Service by presidential proclamation, 14 August 1958.
Two-stage restoration, 1995 to 2000: new lantern room, repointed brickwork, whitewash.
Relit 18 March 2007 with a solar-powered beacon.
Masonry stabilized by a Fort Pulaski preservation team, summer 2021.

corrections.why: LighthouseFriends says the tower was closed for safety reasons in 2015, and the NPS says the lighthouse and its island are closed to the public.
The NPS says the lighthouse and its island are closed to the public; an overlook trail gives the view from land.
The record's access note comes from the USLHS archive, which lists it as open. The NPS, which now owns the island, says it is closed to the public.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The first tower dates from 1837 to 1839 (NPS). The record's 1848 first-lit date comes from Wikidata. NPS dates Norris's contract to 1848, and LighthouseFriends dates the two beacons' establishment to 1849; this file uses 1849 from LighthouseFriends.
The rebuilt tower is dated 1855 (NPS, Bulletin 1934), 1856 (LighthouseFriends) and 1857 (USLHS). Not resolved; the story says so.
The USLHS archive gives a sixth-order Fresnel lens installed 1857. LighthouseFriends gives a fifth-order lens in 1856. Wikipedia's lead, which is not cited, says fourth-order.
The 1934 Bulletin gives 1834, with reappropriation in 1837. LighthouseFriends gives an act of 3 March 1832 for an unlit beacon on the oyster beds.
The NPS describes the first light with five lamps and 14-inch reflectors; LighthouseFriends gives three lamps and 14-inch reflectors for the beacons. The story gives both.
The NPS says the water rose 23 feet above sea level; LighthouseFriends says it rose 23 feet above normal. The story gives both.

notes_for_editor: Confidence is medium because the sources disagree on several dates and measurements, listed in resolved_conflicts. Not resolved: focal height (the record's 12.5 m from the ENC; the USLHS gives 22 ft above mean high water, about 6.7 m; the NPS gives 25 ft above sea level for the 1848 light). Tower height (record 14 m from Wikidata; USLHS 20 ft to the centre of the lantern). The keeper roster runs to 1911, but the light was put out in 1909; the USLHS roster is cited as printed. LighthouseFriends adds John A. Robertson, Jr. (1911-1913) and runs Ohman to 1913; the Robertson line is flagged. George W. Martus: LighthouseFriends says he accepted the station in 1881, the roster has him an assistant from 1877. The story does not use this. Cornelius Maher's drowning (1853) and Thomas Egan's (1871) rest on LighthouseFriends alone; no newspaper or report read here confirms them. A Georgia newspaper search for the 1850s found nothing. No wreck or rescue tied to the station was found in the sources read. The 1900 report passages (items 780-781, 609 for Fort Washington) are cited by scan page; the printed page was not read. The Bulletin 1934 OCR reads 'Ccckspur', 'tbe' and 'III 1880'; quotes are copied as OCR'd. LighthouseFriends is a copyrighted site: its facts are paraphrased, with no more than a phrase quoted. Wikipedia was read for leads only (1837 to 1839 construction; 1854 damage; 1855 rebuild by John S. Norris; fourth-order lens; relit 2007) and is not cited. Position: the USLHS lat/lon (32 01.21 N, 80 52.46 W) differs from the record's OSM point by under a mile; no correction is proposed.
